title: Visualizing the 2D Obstacle Grid and A* Path
description: Define show_grid_path to display the obstacle array with plt.imshow, plot the (x, y) coordinates of path_grid, and mark start "S" and goal "G".
source: draft: agy free model + edit: codex

steps.description: Start `show_grid_path(grid, path=None, start=None, goal=None, title=...)` and display `grid` with `plt.imshow(grid, origin="upper")`. If `path` is given, unpack `ys = [y for (y, x) in path]` and `xs = [x for (y, x) in path]`. Draw `plt.plot(xs, ys, linewidth=3)`.
Plot `start` (`"S"`, marker `"o"`) and `goal` (`"G"`, marker `"x"`), set the title, call `plt.gca().invert_yaxis()`, and invoke `show_grid_path` on `(grid, path_grid, start, goal)`.

Look closely at the coordinate order on lines 8-16: each grid cell is stored as `(row, col) = (y, x)`. `plt.plot(xs, ys)` and `plt.scatter([start[1]], [start[0]])` take horizontal coordinate `x` (`col`) first and vertical coordinate `y` (`row`) second.

steps.question: Why does the start-marker call pass `[start[1]], [start[0]]` to `plt.scatter` instead of `[start[0]], [start[1]]`?
steps.answer: Because `start` is a `(row, col)` tuple `(y, x)`, and Matplotlib's `plt.scatter(x, y)` expects the column index `start[1]` on the x-axis and the row index `start[0]` on the y-axis.
